caption: "first day of fall" — 100,000+ searches this week. Swipe for 10 things most people don't know about the equinox.

Why: the September equinox is the moment the Sun crosses the celestial equator. In 2026 that is September 23 at 00:06 UTC: 8:06 pm September 22 in New York, 7:06 am September 23 in Bangkok. Autumn in the north, spring in the south.

What most people don't know: day and night are not equal on the equinox. The atmosphere bends sunlight and the Sun is a disc, so the day runs about 14 minutes longer at the equator. The truly equal day, the equilux, comes a few days later.
Very simply put: equal night is the name, not the measurement.

slides.headline: The equinox is *not* a day of equal day and night.
slides.sub: 10 things most people don't know about the first day of fall, 100,000+ searches this week.

slides.headline: It happens at *00:06 UTC* on September 23.
slides.sub: 8:06 pm September 22 in New York, 7:06 am September 23 in Bangkok. The Sun crosses the celestial equator, heading south.
slides.image: The sun sitting exactly on a flat sea horizon in clear evening light, sun in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain calm water, photorealistic, no text

slides.headline: The day is about *14 minutes* longer than the night.
slides.sub: At the equator, and more towards the poles. The atmosphere bends sunlight over the horizon and the Sun is a disc, not a point.
slides.image: A sundial casting a long shadow on a stone plinth in a bright garden, sundial in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain gravel, photorealistic, no readable text

slides.headline: The truly equal day, the *equilux*, comes days later.
slides.sub: A few days towards winter at mid-latitudes. The word equinox is Latin: aequus, equal, and nox, night.
slides.image: An old brass balance scale perfectly level on a wooden table in soft window light, scale in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain wood, photorealistic, no text

slides.headline: Everywhere on Earth the Sun rises *due east* today.
slides.sub: And sets due west. It is the one day the compass and the sunrise agree, from Bangkok to Buenos Aires.
slides.image: A vintage brass compass lying on a wooden dock at sunrise, compass in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain weathered planks, photorealistic, no readable text

slides.headline: Seasons come from a *23.4 degree* tilt, not distance.
slides.sub: Earth is closest to the Sun in January and farthest in July. Distance changes the sunlight by only 7%.
slides.image: A classroom globe tilted on its stand, lit from one side against a dark background, globe in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain dark desk, photorealistic, no readable text

slides.headline: South of the equator it is the first day of *spring*.
slides.sub: The hemispheres always sit in opposite seasons. Meteorologists started autumn on September 1 regardless.
slides.image: Pink cherry blossoms against a bright blue spring sky, blossoms in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain sky, photorealistic, no text

slides.headline: It can fall anywhere from *September 21 to 24*.
slides.sub: The calendar year and the Sun's year do not match, so the moment drifts: 2025 was September 22, 2027 will be September 23 at 06:02 UTC.
slides.image: Pages of a paper wall calendar fanned in the breeze on a plain white wall, calendar in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain white, photorealistic, no readable text

slides.headline: Japan gives it a *public holiday*; China eats mooncakes.
slides.sub: Autumnal Equinox Day in Japan. The Mid-Autumn Festival falls on Friday, September 25 this year, on the fullest moon of the harvest.
